title.value: Multicomponent, Multiphase Flow in Porous Media with Temperature Variation

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: The decreasing availability of hydrocarbon reserves exploitable by primary or secondary recovery processes has inspired the development of many different enhanced recovery methods. These methods are often divided into thermal and chemical recovery processes.Thermal recovery by nature is a primary example of multiphase, multicomponent flow accompanied by a temperature gradient. Both steam processes and in-situ combustion are excellent examples of this phenomenon. Simultaneous flow of gas, oil and water at changing temperatures are present in steam injections. In-situ combustion methods generate hot product gases such as CO2 and steam that flow ahead of the combustion front into a cold oil bank. The interaction of the product gases, temperature and oil is a complex system that is not easily open to study.Many types of chemical recovery also exhibit these temperature gradients in addition to complex flow and phase behavior interrelations. Often the reservoir temperature is greater than the temperature of the injected fluids. This temperature difference can be very great in deep formations or where a large geothermal gradients exist. The change in flow and fluid properties as the fluids approach the reservoir temperature is an important issue that merits close examination.The model described in this dissertation is able to consider these interactions in a clear manner. A set of hyperbolic partial differential equations is solved using the method of characteristics. The model takes into account the phase behavior by using an equation of state to partition the individual components into different phases. Temperature effects are accounted for by including an enthalpy balance along with the material balances for each component. Flow effects are modelled by using fractional flow curves and a three phase relative permeability model.Three major problems are studied in this dissertation. Each new problem adds an additional level of interaction to the solution before. The first problem eliminates the phase behavior aspect of the problem by studying the flow of a single component a s it undergoes an isothermal phase change. The second problem couples the effects of temperature and flow behavior by including a second component that is immiscible with the original component. Finally, phase behavior is added by using a set of three partially miscible components that partition into two or three separate phases.Solutions for these equations are formed from spreading waves that propagate in space and time with a constant velocity. The spreading wave regions are connected by jump discontinuities or zones of constant state. The solutions are presented for the three example systems in the form of saturation or composition profiles and solution paths in the composition space. An analysis of the effect of varying some of the important parameters are also presented for each displacement system. The results are summarized in the final chapter. The results are grouped into those that consider the behavior and application of the method of characteristics to the solution of multicomponent, multiphase flow problems that include temperature variation. Limitations to the kinds of systems that the model can describe are discussed.
Wingard, Jeffrey S. (1988). Multicomponent, Multiphase Flow in Porous Media with Temperature Variation. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: https://purl.stanford.edu/nd057rp1412
